gaps: Baseline latency_p95 window (14:50:20–14:52:35) returned empty (ev_3), so pre-incident baseline behavior could only be inferred from the first samples of the incident window.
Error-level log detail search over the incident window was cut off by the tool budget (ev_13, budget_exhausted); pool-timeout messages were not inspected.
A baseline log-pattern comparison was not run, so it is unconfirmed whether "order rejected" is normal for this service.
CPU / eventloop_utilization / memory metrics for the service process were not queried, so CPU saturation and event-loop primacy could not be tested.
Slow-query or per-statement DB metrics and connection-hold times were not queried.
Trace-level span data and deployment/change events around 14:54 were not checked.
summary: HTTP p95 latency on demo-service left a flat baseline in the final two samples, coinciding with the DB pool reaching its maximum and a growing pending queue, elevated DB operation and pool-wait latency, and rising event-loop delay; first 5xx errors appear only at the last sample. Most probable cause: DB pool exhaustion driven by slow database work, with event-loop degradation as the earliest signal and an open alternative that the stall is primary. Baseline comparison and error-log detail were not completed.

timeline.event: Window opens with pool_used at 0 and HTTP latency p95 at baseline ~0.009 s.
Event-loop delay p99 first departs baseline (0.026 s vs ~0.013 s) while pool usage is still 0.
DB pool reaches its ceiling: pool_used 10 of pool_max 10 with 9 pending requests; event-loop delay p99 0.271 s.
DB operation p95 0.437 s, pool wait p95 1.46 s and HTTP latency p95 2.174 s; only the first warn/error log lines exist and 5xx ratio is still 0.
Last sampled "order rejected" warn line, part of a background pattern running since 14:52:44.
Peak degradation and detection point: HTTP p95 2.426 s, pending requests 44, pool wait p95 1.882 s, db operation p95 0.463 s, event-loop delay p99 0.455 s, and the first 5xx error ratio 0.0115.

hypotheses.statement: DB connection pool exhaustion caused the incident: slow database work (db operation p95 up to {db_last}) held all {pool_used_max} pooled connections, queued pending requests up to {pending_last}, drove pool wait p95 to {wait_last} and pushed HTTP p95 latency to {lat_max}.

Event-loop degradation caused the incident: event-loop delay p99 rose first (to {el_at_20} at 14:54:20 and {el_max} by 14:54:50), starving request handling, holding DB connections longer and producing pool saturation and the HTTP latency spike to {lat_max}.
CPU saturation of the service process caused the incident, with event-loop delay p99 peaking at {el_max} and HTTP p95 latency reaching {lat_max} as CPU-bound work stalled request processing.
Elevated downstream database dependency latency caused the incident, with db operation p95 rising to {db_last} and pool wait p95 to {wait_last}, delaying responses up to HTTP p95 {lat_max}.

observations.statement: HTTP latency p95 was flat near 0.009 s through 14:54:20 and then jumped to {lat_onset} at 14:54:35, peaking at {lat_max} at 14:54:50, matching the fired detection rule.

DB connection pool usage was zero until 14:54:05 and then reached the ceiling: pool_used rose to {pool_used_max} connections at 14:54:20 and stayed there, against a constant pool_max of {pool_max} connections.
Pending pool requests went from 0 at 14:54:05 to {pending_at_20} at 14:54:20 and {pending_last} at 14:54:50, showing a queue building while the pool was saturated.
Pool wait latency p95 was about 0.00096 s through 14:54:20 and then rose to {wait_at_35} at 14:54:35 and {wait_last} at 14:54:50.
DB operation p95 was about 0.0048 s through 14:54:20 and then rose to {db_at_35} at 14:54:35 and {db_last} at 14:54:50, i.e. database work slowed at the same time as the pool filled.
Event-loop delay p99 departed its ~0.013 s baseline first, reaching {el_at_20} at 14:54:20 and peaking at {el_max} at 14:54:50 — earlier onset than the pool saturation.
The 5xx error ratio was zero until it reached {err_last} at the final sample (14:54:50), so the event was primarily latency/queueing rather than an error storm.
Request rate stayed in a moderate band throughout the window, peaking at {rps_max} req/s at 14:53:50 and at {rps_last} req/s at 14:54:50, without a spike contemporaneous with the latency jump.
Log patterns show only one pattern, 16 warn "order rejected" lines spanning both service versions and running from 14:52:44 to 14:54:40, i.e. background noise starting before the latency jump.
Log volume in the window included {err_log_sum} error-severity lines in a single bucket and {warn_log_sum} warn-severity lines across three buckets, alongside {info_log_sum} info lines.

recommendations.action: Capture slow-query and connection-hold data for the 14:54:05–14:55:00 period (db_operation_p95 split by statement, longest-running transactions) to identify what held the pooled connections.
recommendations.rationale: hyp_1 attributes the saturation to slow database work; DB operation p95 reached {db_last} while all {pool_used_max} connections were busy.

recommendations.action: Add pool saturation alerting on pool_pending above a small threshold and on pool_used at pool_max so the queue is caught before HTTP p95 breaches.
recommendations.rationale: hyp_1: pool_pending rose from 0 to {pending_last} while pool wait p95 reached {wait_last}, which preceded the user-visible latency peak.

recommendations.action: Check query timeouts / statement timeouts and per-request connection-hold limits so a slow dependency cannot consume the whole pool.
recommendations.rationale: hyp_1: a bounded hold time would cap pool wait p95, which reached {wait_last} seconds.

recommendations.action: Query eventloop_utilization and CPU metrics for 14:54:00–14:54:30 to test whether CPU-bound work caused the event-loop delay p99 of {el_at_20} observed before pool saturation.
recommendations.rationale: hyp_2 and hyp_3 both depend on whether the event-loop degradation was primary; open question after the budget cut off further queries.

recommendations.action: Inspect error-level logs for pool-timeout or connection-acquisition errors around 14:54:50 to confirm the 5xx errors came from queue overflow rather than the downstream database itself.
recommendations.rationale: hyp_4 is an alternative attribution of the latency to the downstream dependency; the 5xx ratio only reached {err_last} at the last sample and error-log detail was not retrieved.
